questions.q: Why does sparse reward bite harder in long-horizon multi-turn agent tasks than in Chapter 5's toy Gymnasium environments?
options: It doesn't; sparsity is equally easy to handle in both settings

Trajectories are longer, spreading credit even thinner (as lesson 61 covered), and the action space at each turn is far larger (open-ended text and tools rather than a handful of discrete moves), making a lucky random success even less likely
Agent tasks never have any reward signal at all
Toy Gymnasium environments have no sparse reward problem to compare against
questions.explain: The combination of longer horizons and a much larger per-turn action space compounds the sparse-reward problem beyond what simple discrete-action environments present.

questions.q: What guarantee does potential-based reward shaping provide, and under what condition does that guarantee hold?
options: It always improves training speed with no conditions attached
Adding γ·Φ(s′) − Φ(s) to the reward does not change which policy is optimal, but only if Φ is a function of state alone, not of the action taken to reach that state
It guarantees the policy will never explore unnecessary tool calls
It only works for episodes shorter than ten turns
questions.explain: The theoretical guarantee behind potential-based shaping (from Chapter 5) depends critically on the potential function depending only on state; a shaping term that depends on the action loses this guarantee.

questions.q: How do subgoal rewards differ from formal potential-based shaping, according to this lesson?
options: They are mathematically identical with no practical difference

Subgoal rewards are ad hoc partial rewards for milestones believed to correlate with success, chosen because identifying a true potential function is often harder, but they give up the optimality guarantee entirely
Subgoal rewards always provide a stronger optimality guarantee than potential-based shaping
Subgoal rewards cannot be used in agentic RL environments at all
questions.explain: Subgoal rewards are more common in practice for convenience, but unlike potential-based shaping they carry no formal guarantee that optimizing them still optimizes the true task objective.

questions.q: What risk does the lesson identify with stacking multiple subgoal rewards into one training run?
options: Subgoal rewards have no risk at all since they are always correlated with success
Each additional subgoal reward is a chance for the policy to learn to farm that specific signal rather than genuinely progress toward the real goal, and this risk compounds with every added subgoal
Subgoal rewards can only be added one at a time, never stacked
Stacking subgoal rewards always slows down training with no other effect
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames every added shaping or subgoal signal as an additional opportunity for reward hacking, with the risk compounding as more such signals are introduced.

questions.q: What practical training strategy does the lesson recommend for balancing learning speed against the risk of shaping-induced reward hacking?
options: Always use the maximum possible number of subgoal rewards from the very start of training

Start with sparse-only training on an easier task distribution to get a working baseline, then introduce shaping carefully and re-check with the evaluation discipline from lesson 59 whether the policy is genuinely better or just better at collecting shaped reward
Never use any form of reward shaping under any circumstances
Only use shaped rewards and never evaluate the resulting policy
questions.explain: The lesson recommends a staged approach — sparse baseline first, careful shaping second, with evaluation checks to distinguish real improvement from reward-shaping artifacts.
